{{Use American English|date=March 2021}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=March 2021}}
[[File:Tyre Arm Chair.jpg|thumb|Tire arm chair]]
[[File:Holice, hromada pneumatik (01).jpg|thumb|240px|right|Tires are among the most problematic sources of waste. Progress in recycling has resulted in a major reduction in dumping.]]

'''Tire recycling''', or '''rubber recycling''', is the process of [[recycling]] waste [[tire]]s that are no longer suitable for use on vehicles due to wear or irreparable damage. These tires are a challenging source of waste, due to the large volume produced, the durability of the tires, and the components in the tire that are ecologically problematic.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |url=https://rma.org/sites/default/files/EPA_Scrap_Tire_Handbook_on_Recycling_Management.pdf |title=Scrap Tires: Handbook on Recycling Applications and Management for the U.S. and Mexico |date=December 2010 |website=epa.gov |publisher=United States Environmental Protection Agency |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161117211239/https://rma.org/sites/default/files/EPA_Scrap_Tire_Handbook_on_Recycling_Management.pdf |archive-date=17 November 2016}}</ref>

Because tires are highly durable and non-biodegradable, they can consume valuable space in landfills.<ref name=":0"/> If waste tires are improperly managed they may cause [[rubber pollution]]. In 1990, it was estimated that over 1 billion scrap tires were in stockpiles in the United States. As of 2015, only 67 million tires remain in stockpiles.<ref name=":1">{{cite news |url=https://rma.org/scrap-tire/scrap-tire-markets/stockpile-cleanup/ |title=Stockpile Cleanup |date=15 March 2016 |newspaper=Rubber Manufacturers Association |access-date=17 November 2016 |via=Google Scholar |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161117211512/https://rma.org/scrap-tire/scrap-tire-markets/stockpile-cleanup/ |archive-date=17 November 2016}}</ref> From 1994 to 2010, the European Union increased the amount of tires recycled from 25% of annual discards to nearly 95%, with roughly half of the end-of-life tires used for energy, mostly in cement manufacturing.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.etrma.org/uploads/Modules/Documentsmanager/brochure-elt-2011-final.pdf |title=End of Life Tyres: A Valuable Resource with Growing Potential |date=2011 |publisher=European Tyre and Rubber Manufacturers' Association |access-date=16 November 2016 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151123184917/http://www.etrma.org/uploads/Modules/Documentsmanager/brochure-elt-2011-final.pdf |archive-date=23 November 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sienkiewicz |first1=Maciej |last2=Kucinska-Lipka |first2=Justyna |last3=Janik |first3=Helena |last4=Balas |first4=Adolf |title=Progress in used tyres management in the European Union: A review |journal=Waste Management |date=October 2012 |volume=32 |issue=10 |pages=1742–1751 |doi=10.1016/j.wasman.2012.05.010 |pmid=22687707 |bibcode=2012WaMan..32.1742S}}</ref>

[[Pyrolysis]] and de[[vulcanization]] could facilitate recycling. Aside from use as fuel, the main end use for tires remains ground [[crumb rubber]].<ref name=":1"/><ref name=RubCh>{{cite journal |last1=Myhre |first1=Marvin |last2=Saiwari |first2=Sitisaiyidah |last3=Dierkes |first3=Wilma |last4=Noordermeer |first4=Jacques |journal=Rubber Chemistry and Technology |volume=85 |issue=3 |pages=408–449 |doi=10.5254/rct.12.87973 |year=2012 |title=Rubber Recycling: Chemistry, Processing, and Applications}}</ref> In 2017, 13% of [[tire recycling in the United States|U.S. tires]] removed from their primary use were sold in the used tire market. Of the tires that were scrapped, 43% were burnt as [[tire-derived fuel]], with cement manufacturing the largest user, another 25% were used to make ground rubber, 8% were used in civil engineering projects, 17% were disposed of in landfills and 8% had other uses.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ustires.org/system/files/USTMA_scraptire_summ_2017_072018.pdf |title=2017 U.S. Scrap Tire Management Summary |date=18 July 2018 |publisher=U.S. Tire Manufacturers Association |access-date=25 July 2019 |archive-date=12 February 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190212130744/https://www.ustires.org/system/files/USTMA_scraptire_summ_2017_072018.pdf |url-status=dead}}</ref> Globally, tire graveyards are a common environmental hazard, with significant pollutants and other challenges. For example, the [[Sulaibiya]] tire graveyard in Kuwait has had repeat highly [[tire fire|toxic fires]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Technologies |first=Mano |title=EPA To Remove Tires From Site, Hand Over Land To PAHW Soon {{!}} Kuwait Local |url=https://kuwaitlocal.com/news/epa-to-remove-tires-from-site-hand-over-land-to-pahw-soon |access-date=2023-01-06 |website=Kuwaitlocal |language=en}}</ref>

==Tire life cycle==
The tire life cycle can be recognized through the following steps:
#Product developments and innovations such as improved compounds and camber tire shaping increase tire life, increments of replacement, consumer safety, and reduce tire waste.
#Proper manufacturing and quality of delivery reduces waste at production.
# Direct distribution through retailers, reduces inventory time and ensures that the life span and the safety of the products are explained to customers.
# Consumers' use and maintenance choices like [[tire rotation]] and alignment affect tire wear and safety of operation.
# Manufacturers and retailers set policies on return, [[retread]], and replacement to reduce the waste generated from tires and assume responsibility for taking the 'tire to its grave' or to its reincarnation.
#Recycling tires by developing strategies that combust or process waste into new products, creates viable businesses, and fulfilling public policies.<ref name="Price, Willard 2006">{{cite journal |doi=10.1504/IJETM.2006.009001 |title=Waste tire recycling: Environmental benefits and commercial challenges |journal=International Journal of Environmental Technology and Management |volume=6 |issue=3/4 |pages=362 |year=2006 |last1=Price |first1=Willard |last2=Smith |first2=Edgar D.}}</ref>
[[File:Debris left on the refuge in the wake of hurricane Katrina.jpg|thumb|Tires in a natural area after [[Hurricane Katrina]] created debris. Tires left in landfills and other waste retention areas are likely to enter the environment during flooding or other [[extreme weather]] events.]]

==Landfill disposal==
Tires are not desired at [[landfill]]s, due to their large volumes and 75% void space.<ref name="Liu, H. 1998">Liu, H., Mead, J., Stacer, R. Chelsea Center For Recycling And Economic Development. (1998). Environmental Impacts of Recycling Rubber in Light Fill Applications: Summary & Evaluation of Existing Literature University of Massachusetts</ref> Tires can trap [[methane]] gases, causing them to become buoyant, or [[landfill gas migration|bubble]] to the surface. This 'bubbling' effect can damage [[landfill liner]]s that have been installed to help keep landfill contaminants from polluting local surface and [[ground water]].<ref name="Price, Willard 2006"/> The EU [[Landfill Directive]] prohibits the disposal of used tires in landfill.<ref>[http://www.environment-agency.gov.uk/business/sectors/37223.aspx The Environment Agency] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130202222655/http://environment-agency.gov.uk/business/sectors/37223.aspx |date=2 February 2013}}</ref>

Shredded tires are now being used in landfills, replacing other construction materials, for a lightweight back-fill in gas venting systems, [[leachate]] collection systems, and operational liners. Shredded tire material may also be used to cap, close, or daily cover landfill sites.<ref name="epa">{{cite web |url=http://www.epa.gov/osw/conserve/materials/tires/basic.htm |title=Scrap Tires – Basic Information |date=16 July 2011 |access-date=22 September 2011 |publisher=US Environmental Protection Agency |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111023123908/http://www.epa.gov/osw/conserve/materials/tires/basic.htm |archive-date=23 October 2011}}</ref> Scrap tires as a back-fill and cover material are also more cost-effective, since tires can be shredded on-site instead of hauling in other fill materials.

==Stockpiles and legal dumping==
[[File:Tires and shredded.JPG|thumb|right|Used tires in the foreground, waiting to be shredded. A pile of shredded tires in the background.]]
Tire stockpiles create a great health and safety risk. [[Tire fire]]s can easily occur, burning for long periods, up to a month and also creating substantial [[air pollution|pollution in the air]] and [[soil pollution|ground]]. Recycling helps to reduce the number of tires in storage. An additional health risk, tire piles provide harborage for vermin and a breeding ground for [[mosquito]]es that may carry diseases. [[Illegal dumping]] of scrap tires pollutes ravines, woods, deserts, and empty lots; which has led many states to pass scrap tire regulations requiring proper management. Tire amnesty day events, in which community members can deposit a limited number of waste tires free of charge, can be funded by state scrap tire programs, helping decrease illegal dumping and improper storage of scrap tires.

Tire storage and recycling are sometimes linked with illegal activities and lack of [[environmental awareness]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-devon-17195524 |title=Crumb Rubber told to move rubble it dumped in Devon woodland |date=28 February 2012 |via=BBC |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140303211802/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-devon-17195524 |archive-date=3 March 2014 |work=BBC News}}</ref>

==Uses==
[[File:Tire Flower Planters in Sunnyside, Queens, NYC 2026.jpg|alt=Tires painted red, blue, turquoise, and yellow are used as flower planters in a front yard |thumb|Tire flower planters in Queens, NY]]
Although tires are usually burnt, not recycled, efforts are continuing to find value. Tires can be reclaimed into, among other things, hot-melt [[bitumen|asphalt]], typically as [[crumb rubber]] modifier—recycled asphalt pavement (CRM—RAP),<ref>Kandhal PS. (1992). [http://ntl.bts.gov/lib/6000/6400/6407/rep92-6.pdf WASTE MATERIALS IN HOT MIX ASPHALT – AN OVERVIEW] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090513181152/http://ntl.bts.gov/lib/6000/6400/6407/rep92-6.pdf |date=13 May 2009}}. National Center for Asphalt Technology.</ref><ref>T. E. Baker (2003). [http://www.wsdot.wa.gov/biz/mats/Draft%20Final%20Report%20Version%205.pdf Evaluation of the Use of Scrap Tires in Transportation Related Applications in the State of Washington] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110610051824/http://www.wsdot.wa.gov/biz/mats/Draft%20Final%20Report%20Version%205.pdf |date=10 June 2011}}</ref> and as an aggregate in [[Portland cement]] [[concrete]]<ref>M Nehdi, A Khan, (2001). [http://www.bvsde.paho.org/bvsacd/cd24/cementi.pdf Cementitious Composites Containing Recycled Tire Rubber: An Overview of Engineering Properties and Potential Applications] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110724084425/http://www.bvsde.paho.org/bvsacd/cd24/cementi.pdf |date=24 July 2011}}. ''Cement, Concrete, and Aggregates''.</ref> Efforts have been made to use recycled tires as raw material for new tires, but such tires may integrate recycled materials no more than 5% by weight, and tires that contain recycled material are inferior to new tires,<ref name=RubCh/> suffering from reduced tread life and lower traction.<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.calrecycle.ca.gov/publications/Documents/Tires%5C62204001.doc |title=Increasing the Recycled Content in New Tires |contribution=California Integrated Waste Management Board |contribution-url=http://www.calrecycle.ca.gov/ |access-date=1 October 2017 |year=2004 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170210215448/http://www.calrecycle.ca.gov/Publications/Documents/Tires/62204001.doc |archive-date=10 February 2017}}</ref> Tires have also been cut up and used in garden beds as bark mulch to hold in the water and to prevent weeds from growing. Some "green" buildings, both private and public, have been made from old tires.

[[Pyrolysis]] can be used to reprocess the tires into [[fuel gas]], oils, solid residue (char), and low-grade [[carbon black]], which cannot be used in tire manufacture. A pyrolysis method which produces [[activated carbon]] and high-grade carbon black has been suggested.<ref>Wojtowicz MA, Serio MA. (1996). [http://www.afrinc.com/NGE/CHEMTECH_26_10_48-53_1996.pdf Pyrolysis of scrap tires: Can it be profitable?] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140912182631/http://www.afrinc.com/NGE/CHEMTECH_26_10_48-53_1996.pdf |date=12 September 2014}}. ''Chemtech''.</ref>

===Cement manufacturing===
[[File:LDWisconsinTireInject.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Used tires being fed mid-kiln to a pair of long [[cement kiln]]s]]
Old tires can be used as an alternative fuel in the manufacturing of [[Portland cement]], a key ingredient in concrete. Whole tires are commonly introduced into [[cement kiln]]s, by rolling them into the upper end of a preheater kiln, or by dropping them through a slot midway along a long wet kiln. In either case, the high gas temperatures (1000–1200 °C) cause almost instantaneous, complete and smokeless combustion of the tire. Alternatively, tires are chopped into 5–10 mm chips, in which form they can be injected into a precalciner combustion chamber. Some iron input is required in manufacturing cement, so the iron content of steel-belted tires is beneficial to the process.<ref>[http://www.seas.columbia.edu/earth/wtert/sofos/MEQ-01-2015-0012.pdf Use of waste derived fuels in cement industry: a review] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161024155044/http://www.seas.columbia.edu/earth/wtert/sofos/MEQ-01-2015-0012.pdf |date=24 October 2016}}, Nickolaos Chatziaras, Constantinos S. Psomopoulos, Nickolas J. Themelis, 2016, Management of Environmental Quality: An International Journal, Vol. 27 Iss 2 pp. 178 – 193, https://dx.doi.org/10.1108/MEQ-01-2015-0012, 8 March 2016</ref>

===Tire-derived products===
[[File:Shredded tires.JPG|thumb|right|Shredded tires]]
[[File:Double Shaft Tire Shredder.jpg|thumb|Tires can be shredded into small blocks for fuel with a tire shredder.]]
[[File:Shredded tires2.JPG|thumb|right|Closeup of shredded tires]]
[[File:Tire Crumb.JPG|thumb|right|1 ton bags of [[crumb rubber]]]]

Tires can be reused in many ways, although most used tires are burnt for their [[tire-derived fuel|fuel]] value.<ref name="Bandy">{{cite journal |last2=Agrawal |first2=S.L. |last3=Ameta |first3=R. |last4=Dasgupta |first4=S. |last5=Mukhopadhyay |first5=R. |last6=Deuri |first6=A.S. |last7=Ameta |first7=Suresh C. |last8=Ameta |first8=Rakshit |year=2008 |title=An overview of rubber recycling |journal=Progress in Rubber, Plastics and Recycling Technology |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=73–112 |last1=Bandyopadhyay |first1=S. |doi=10.1177/147776060802400201 |s2cid=138225336}}</ref> In a 2003 report cited by the U.S. [[EPA]], it is stated that markets ("both recycling and beneficial use") existed for 80.4% of scrap tires, about 233 million tires per year. Assuming {{convert|22.5|lbs}} per tire, the 2003 report predicts a total weight of about {{convert|2.62|e6t}}<!--unclear: metric or imperial or worse?--> from tires.<ref>22.5 lb working figure retrieved on 20 February 2010 from: {{cite web |url=http://www.rma.org/scrap_tires/scrap_tire_markets/scrap_tire_characteristics |title=Rubber Manufacturers Association |access-date=21 February 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100305071346/http://www.rma.org/scrap%5Ftires/scrap%5Ftire%5Fmarkets/scrap%5Ftire%5Fcharacteristics/ |archive-date=5 March 2010}}/</ref>

New products derived from waste tires generate more economic activity than [[combustion]] or other low multiplier production, while reducing waste stream without generating excessive pollution and emissions from recycling operations.<ref name="Price, Willard 2006"/>

*Construction materials. Entire homes can be built with whole tires by filling them with earth and covering them with concrete, a common material in [[earthship]]s. They are used in civil engineering applications such as sub-grade fill and embankments, [[back-fill]] for walls and bridge abutments, sub-grade insulation for roads, [[landfill]] projects, and septic system drain fields. Tires are also bound together and used as different types of barriers such as: collision reduction, [[erosion control]], rainwater runoff, [[blasting mat]]s, wave action that protects piers and marshes, and sound barriers between roadways and residences.
*[[Artificial reef]]s are built using tires that are bonded together in groups. There is some controversy on how effective tires are as an artificial reef system; an example is The [[Osborne Reef]] Project which has become an environmental nightmare that will cost millions of dollars to rectify.
*The process of stamping and cutting tires is used in some apparel products, such as sandals and as a road sub-base, by connecting together the cut sidewalls to form a flexible net.
*The markets predicted by the 2003 report were: [[tire-derived fuel]] (TDF) using 130 million tires, civil engineering projects using 56 million tires, ground rubber turned into molded rubber products using 18 million tires, ground rubber turned into rubber-modified asphalt using 12 million tires, Exported items using 9 million tires, cut, stamped and punched products using 6.5 million tires, and agricultural and miscellaneous uses 3 million tires.<ref name="epa"/>
*Shredded tires, known as [[tire-derived aggregate]] (TDA), have many civil engineering applications. TDA can be used as a back-fill for retaining walls, fill for [[landfill gas]] trench collection wells, back-fill for roadway landslide repair projects as well as a vibration damping material for railway lines.
*Ground and crumb rubber, also known as size-reduced rubber, can be used in both paving type projects and in mold-able products. These types of paving are: [[Rubber Modified Asphalt]] (RMA), [[Rubber Modified Concrete]], and as a substitution for an aggregate. Examples of rubber-molded products are carpet padding or [[underlay]], flooring materials, dock bumpers, patio decks, railroad crossing blocks, livestock mats, sidewalks, rubber tiles and bricks, movable speed bumps, and curbing/edging. The rubber can be molded with plastic for products like pallets and [[railroad tie]]s. Athletic and recreational areas can also be paved with the shock absorbing rubber-molded material. Rubber from tires is sometimes ground into medium-sized chunks and used as [[rubber mulch]]. Rubber crumb can also be used as an infill, alone or blended with coarse sand, as in infill for grass-like synthetic turf products such as Field-turf.
*[[Steel mill]]s can use tires as a carbon source, replacing coal or coke in steel manufacturing.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://crca.asn.au/green-steel-from-old-rubber-tyres-produces-no-waste-or-toxic-fumes/ |title='Green steel' from old rubber tyres produces no waste or toxic fumes – CRC Association |date=16 May 2012 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140814101443/http://crca.asn.au/green-steel-from-old-rubber-tyres-produces-no-waste-or-toxic-fumes/ |archive-date=14 August 2014}}</ref>
*Tires are also often recycled for use on basketball courts and new shoe products.

===Tire pyrolysis===
[[File:Cryopolymers (95-557-24).jpeg|thumb|NASA Stennis Space Center worked on [[cryogenics|cryogenic]] recycling of tires, in 1995.]]
The [[pyrolysis]] method for recycling used tires is a technique which heats whole or shredded tires in a reactor vessel containing an oxygen-free atmosphere. In the reactor, the rubber is softened after which the rubber polymers [[depolymerization|break down into smaller molecules]]. These smaller molecules eventually [[vaporize]] and exit from the reactor. These vapors can be burned directly to produce power or condensed into an oily type liquid, generally used as a [[fuel]]. Some molecules are too small to condense. They remain as a gas which can be burned as fuel. The minerals that were part of the tire, about 40% by weight, are removed as solid [[ash]]es. When performed properly, the ''tire pyrolysis'' process is a clean operation and produces little emissions or waste; however, concerns about [[air pollution]] due to [[incomplete combustion]] as is the case with [[tire fire]]s has been documented.<ref>{{cite web |publisher=EPA |title=Burning Tires for Fuel and Tire Pyrolysis: Air Implications |year=1991 |url=https://nepis.epa.gov/Exe/ZyPURL.cgi?Dockey=9100LGXA.txt |access-date=4 April 2016 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160416124937/http://nepis.epa.gov/Exe/ZyPURL.cgi?Dockey=9100LGXA.txt |archive-date=16 April 2016}}</ref>

[[File:Three Boys on a Tire Swing.JPG|thumb|Three boys are on a tire swing]]
The properties of the gas, liquid, and solid output are determined by the type of feed-stock used and the process conditions. For instance whole tires contain fibers and steel. Shredded tires have most of the steel and sometimes most of the fiber removed. Processes can be either batch or continuous. The energy required to drive the [[decomposition]] of the rubber include using directly fired fuel (like a [[gas oven]]), electrical induction (like an electrically heated oven) or by [[microwave]]s (like a microwave oven). Sometimes a [[catalyst]] is used to accelerate the decomposition. The choice of feed-stock and process can affect the value of the finished products.
[[File:Car tires as seats in Thailand.JPG|thumb|right|Car tires as seats in Thailand]]The historical issue of tire pyrolysis has been the solid mineral stream, which accounts for about 40% of the output. The [[steel]] can be removed from the solid stream with magnets for recycling. The remaining solid material, often referred to as "[[Char (chemistry)|char]]", has had little or no value other than possibly as a low grade [[carbon-based fuel|carbon fuel]]. Char is the destroyed remains of the original [[carbon black]] used to reinforce and provide abrasion resistance to the tire. The solid stream also includes the minerals used in [[rubber]] manufacturing. This high volume component of tire pyrolysis is a major impediment, although this theme continues to be a source of innovation.
[[File:Tire art.JPG|thumb|right|Tire art]]

===Cryogenic recycling===
Tires can be frozen using [[cryogenics|cryogens]], or super-cold fluids, then broken down and made into [[crumb rubber]] which can be used in asphalt road beds, agricultural hoses, and truck bed liners.

===Repurposing===
[[File:Tires recycled into water tanks on roof. Cherchen, Xinjiang.jpg|thumb|Tires recycled into water tanks on roof. [[Cherchen]], Xinjiang.]]

Aside from recycling old tires, the old tire can be put to a new use.

Old tires are sometimes converted into a [[Swing (seat)|swing]] for play. The innovative use allows for an easy way to find a purpose for an existing old tire not suitable for road use.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.popularmechanics.com/home/how-to-plans/backyard-tire-swing-project |publisher=[[Popular Mechanics]] |title=One Day Project: Kid's Backyard Tire Swing |access-date=1 April 2013 |first=Harry |last=Sawyers |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130405010910/http://www.popularmechanics.com/home/how-to-plans/backyard-tire-swing-project |archive-date=5 April 2013 |date=30 April 2010}}</ref>

Used tires are also employed as exercise equipment for athletic programs such as [[American football]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://football.about.com/od/Football-Conditioning/a/Football-Tire-Drills.htm |publisher=About.com |title=No Frills Football Conditioning |first=Sean |last=McCormick |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130403200128/http://football.about.com/od/Football-Conditioning/a/Football-Tire-Drills.htm |archive-date=3 April 2013}}</ref> One classic conditioning drill that hones players' speed and agility is the "Tire Run" where tires are laid out side by side, with each tire on the left a few inches ahead of the tire on the right in a zigzag pattern. Athletes then run through the tire pattern by stepping in the center of each tire. The drill forces athletes to lift their feet above the ground higher than normal to avoid tripping.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.livestrong.com/article/317036-football-tire-drills/#ixzz2PFqqQ6Wa |publisher=[[LiveStrong]] |title=Football Tire Drills |access-date=1 April 2013 |date=24 November 2010 |first=Jae |last=Ireland |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130605102755/http://www.livestrong.com/article/317036-football-tire-drills/#ixzz2PFqqQ6Wa |archive-date=5 June 2013}}</ref> Other athletic uses include tire flipping (tractor or large truck tires typically used) or for upper cardio conditioning by hitting a tire repetitively with a sledge hammer.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.mensjournal.com/health-fitness/sledgehammer-training/ |title=Sledgehammer Training |newspaper=Men's Journal |access-date=19 October 2018 |date=24 May 2011}}</ref>

Re-purposed tires can also be harnessed as an affordable alternative building material used in the framework of rammed Earth thermal mass dwellings.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://earthship.com/codes-and-laws |title=Earthship – Codes and Laws |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131212123909/http://earthship.com/codes-and-laws |archive-date=12 December 2013}}</ref> This is beneficial across scales of production such as individually sustainable housing.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://earthship.com/media-resume |title=Earthship – Media Resume for Michael E. Reynolds |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131212124258/http://earthship.com/media-resume |archive-date=12 December 2013}}</ref>

Rows of stacks of tires are often used as barriers in motor racing circuits as a method of dissipating kinetic energy over a longer period of time during a crash, comparatively to striking a less malleable material such as a concrete or steel wall.
[[File:Tire repurposed as an elastic base for multipurpose uses.jpg|thumb|Tire repurposed as an elastic base uses. Prototype Nr.2, Variant Nr.1: Mid-body axle swing sign. Lisbon, Portugal.]]

Many cattle farmers re-purpose old tractor tires as water troughs for their cattle by placing them over natural springs or by piping stream water into them. These tires contain the water and allow it to pool for the cattle without any additional interaction from the farmer. Most farmers also include a drainage pipe near the top or in the center of the tire so excess water can drain off to prevent overflow and erosion around the outside of the tire where the cattle would be.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.edenshalefarm.com/blog/giant-rubber-tire-water-tanks |title=Eden Shale Farm}}</ref>

Repurposing as an elastic base for multipurpurposes uses, such as holding advertisement boards, static or swinging. This is an application still under development and at a prototype stage.<ref>{{cite web |title=Mário Brito on LinkedIn: An exercise on Circular Economy: Repurposing of a worn tyre for reuse as... |url=https://www.linkedin.com/posts/m%C3%A1rio-brito-481b8371_an-exercise-on-circular-economy-repurposing-activity-7036005612798787585-qeN3 |access-date=2023-03-10 |website=linkedin.com |language=en}}</ref>

====Rubber shingle roofs====
[[Rubber roof (shingle)|Rubber shingle roofs]] are typically made from 95% recycled material from a variety of sources including recycled tires. They last twice as long as asphalt shingles but are about twice the price as asphalt. They are more quiet than most roofs, hail resistant, and a high wind rating if there is a [[tongue and groove]] fitting at the front edge of the rubber shingle design.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://modernize.com/roof/shingles/rubber |title=Rubber Roofing Shingles | 2023 Cost Guide}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F99d5JN9un0&t=373s |title=Possibly THE MOST Hail Resistant Roof! |website=[[YouTube]]}}</ref>

==Environmental concerns==
Due to their [[Heavy metal (chemistry)|heavy metal]] and other pollutant content, tires pose a risk for the [[leachate|leaching]] of toxins [[infiltration (hydrology)|into]] the [[groundwater]] when placed in [[soil moisture|wet soils]].{{Citation needed|date=February 2025|reason=no source provided for this statement; very little research seems to be available on pollutants leeched from old tires generally, or on said pollutants being a major concern for the environment; most environmental concerns seem to regard buoyancy, gas capture and creating breeding grounds for mosquito populations; the cited portions of this section also further contradict the statement}} Research has shown that very little leaching occurs when shredded tires are used as light fill material; however, limitations have been put on use of this material; each site should be individually assessed determining if this product is appropriate for given conditions.<ref name="Liu, H. 1998"/>

For both above and below water table applications, the preponderance of evidence shows that TDA (tire-derived aggregate, or shredded tires) will not cause primary drinking water standards to be exceeded for metals. Moreover, TDA is unlikely to increase levels of metals with primary drinking water standards above naturally occurring background levels.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://rma.org/sites/default/files/LEA-013-Literature_Review_of_the_Water_Quality_Effects_of_Tire_Derived_Aggregate_and_Rubber_Modified_Asphalt_Pavement.pdf |title=Latest News, Stories & Opinions: Drug Rehab & Alcohol Rehab |access-date=29 November 2016 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161130041005/https://rma.org/sites/default/files/LEA-013-Literature_Review_of_the_Water_Quality_Effects_of_Tire_Derived_Aggregate_and_Rubber_Modified_Asphalt_Pavement.pdf |archive-date=30 November 2016}}</ref>

[[Category:Vehicle recycling]]
extract:
Tire recycling, or rubber recycling, is the process of recycling waste tires that are no longer suitable for use on vehicles due to wear or irreparable damage. These tires are a challenging source of waste, due to the large volume produced, the durability of the tires, and the components in the tire that are ecologically problematic.
Because tires are highly durable and non-biodegradable, they can consume valuable space in landfills. If waste tires are improperly managed they may cause rubber pollution. In 1990, it was estimated that over 1 billion scrap tires were in stockpiles in the United States. As of 2015, only 67 million tires remain in stockpiles. From 1994 to 2010, the European Union increased the amount of tires recycled from 25% of annual discards to nearly 95%, with roughly half of the end-of-life tires used for energy, mostly in cement manufacturing.
Pyrolysis and devulcanization could facilitate recycling. Aside from use as fuel, the main end use for tires remains ground crumb rubber. In 2017, 13% of U.S. tires removed from their primary use were sold in the used tire market. Of the tires that were scrapped, 43% were burnt as tire-derived fuel, with cement manufacturing the largest user, another 25% were used to make ground rubber, 8% were used in civil engineering projects, 17% were disposed of in landfills and 8% had other uses. Globally, tire graveyards are a common environmental hazard, with significant pollutants and other challenges. For example, the Sulaibiya tire graveyard in Kuwait has had repeat highly toxic fires.
